content.text: UNIVERSAL

EIGHT-AXIS COVENANT
ALIGNMENT SYSTEM
Four profile axes • Four expression axes • Four phases • 0–3000 scoring
Built from the attached Universal Alignment System
Original attribution retained: William Saville, also known as The Transgender T-Rex  #TheTransgenderTRex
Version 3.0.0  •  July 2026
NAVIGATION
How to Use This Book
A fast path for play, followed by complete deity, class, and profile references.
PART I
Best Features Only
The strongest ideas from major alignment, belief, honor, corruption, reputation, and faction systems—combined without their unnecessary duplication.
Moral identity: the eight alignment axes.
Personal belief: Convictions and Ties.
External obligation: Duties, class Practices, deity Edicts, and Anathemas.
Divine relationship: Resonance and Claim.
Social judgment: Fame, Faction Standing, Cultural Honor, Legal Status, and Personal Trust.
Psychological injury or supernatural contamination: tracked by their own campaign systems, never treated as proof of evil.
PART II
Quick Start
A complete character can be aligned in five minutes without choosing a permanent moral box.
Set all eight axes to 1500.
Apply background adjustments of up to 250 points on no more than two axes.

Choose a deity covenant only when the character worships, bargains with, serves, resists, or receives class power from that deity. Select up to three suggested pressures and adjust each by no more than 250 points; the player chooses the direction actually supported by the backstory.
Apply the class discipline to up to two listed focus axes, no more than 250 points each. A class never changes an axis merely because its name suggests a personality.
Choose two Convictions, one Tie, one Duty, and one Temptation. One Conviction may begin Defining; the others normally begin Minor or Major.
Convert only the first four axes to low, neutral, or high to find the existing 81-profile title. Append the last four axis descriptors as an expression line.
Deity-powered class characters begin with Covenant Resonance 3 (Attuned) and Divine Claim 0 (Free).
PART III
The Eight Axes and Four Phases
The original profile remains intact while four expression axes add moral and behavioral depth.

content.text: Only the original four axes generate the named profile. The four new axes create a readable expression line. This preserves the complete 81-name registry while allowing two characters with the same title to differ sharply in mercy, attitude toward transformation, source of authority, and self-control.

content.text: PART IV
Convictions, Ties, Duties, Temptations, Resolve, and Strain
Alignment shows the pattern. These elements explain what the character actually believes and what can pull them away from it.
Gain 1 Resolve when a Conviction, Tie, Duty, or Temptation creates a meaningful complication, sacrifice, danger, or lost opportunity that the player accepts. Maximum 3.
Spend 1 Resolve to add 1d6 after a d20 roll, or to resist a Divine Claim complication when the DM allows.
No Resolve is gained for declaring a belief without accepting a cost. Repeated trivial complications cannot be farmed.

A character may want one thing, owe another, believe a third, and be tempted by a fourth. A Covenant Aegis can love an individual, owe a house, serve Nebyrr, and believe coerced unity is evil. The conflict is the point; no single meter decides the answer in advance.
PART V
XP, Axis Movement, and Choice Adjudication
Equal rewards for reinforcement and change; transparent rulings; no grindable morality.
Identify the meaningful choice, not every action taken during the scene.
Record intent and the information reasonably available at the time.
Ask how free the choice was: voluntary, pressured, coerced, compelled, or impossible to avoid.
Judge cost, risk, and foreseeable consequence.
Judge actual consequence separately; unforeseeable harm matters less than knowingly accepted harm.
Identify every axis genuinely demonstrated. Do not move an axis because a class, deity, spell, or faction name merely suggests it.
Apply Roleplay XP and axis movement independently, then update Conviction Strain, Resonance, Claim, or reputation only when their own triggers apply.
State the ruling in one sentence and record it. Resolve extended disagreement after the scene.

content.text: No movement for filler dialogue or harmless repetition.
Normally one award per axis per scene unless separate consequential decisions occur.
Repeated conduct matters again only when stakes, cost, audience, or consequence changes.
A deity bounty cannot increase Resonance more than once per session unless a campaign-defining event justifies it.
The same creature, event, or object cannot be recycled to farm Ichor, alignment, Resolve, or Resonance.
PART VI
The Divine Covenant
Deities influence play through actionable doctrine, Bounty Ichor, Resonance, temptation, miracles, and predatory Claim—not by assigning a compulsory alignment.
Gain: Complete a deity edict or class bounty under meaningful stakes, normally no more than once per session.
Loss: Freely violate an anathema or repeatedly embody the deity's shadow.
Gain: Accept direct miracles, bargains, shadow-driven power, or power beyond ordinary limits.
Loss: Resist divine pressure at meaningful cost, complete a severance rite, or choose autonomy when obedience would be easier.

Every class shapes play through Practices, Hazards, focus axes, its canonical deity, and its exact Bounty trigger.

At levels 1, 5, 11, and 17, choose or strengthen one Class Conviction. A multiclass character tracks one Duty for each class but uses only the covenant of the class whose deity grants the relevant feature.

PART IX
Reputation, Honor, Status, and Faction Standing
Inner alignment is not omniscient public knowledge. Social consequences belong to specific observers and institutions.
PART X
Conversion and Compatibility
Translate old alignment, trait, honor, corruption, and MMO reputation material without collapsing different concepts into one score.

Complete 81-Profile Registry
The original four-axis titles and descriptions remain the readable identity summary. The new axes are appended separately.
APPENDICES
Reference Sheets and Session Record
Compact rules for the table, character sheet, and campaign log.

Universal alignment is a history of choices, not a prison of labels. The profile title makes the character readable; the expression axes make the character specific; Convictions and Ties explain what matters; Duties and Temptations create conflict; deities and classes exert real mechanical pressure; Resonance and Claim make divine power consequential; and reputation records what particular societies believe. None of these substitutes for the player’s next decision.

Canonical scope
This edition uses the twenty-two attached Universal deities as its only pantheon and integrates all twenty-two attached canonical merged classes through one-to-one deity covenants, class practices, hazards, bounties, Resonance, and Divine Claim.
The Eight Axes and Four Phases
Convictions, Ties, Duties, Temptations, Resolve, and Strain
XP, Axis Movement, and Choice Adjudication
The Divine Covenant: Resonance and Claim
Reputation, Honor, Status, and Faction Standing

Fastest play path
Read Part II, record eight starting scores, choose two Convictions, one Tie, one Duty, and one Temptation, then use the one-page scoring procedure in Part V. Deity- or class-powered characters also begin at Resonance 3 and Claim 0.

Alignment records choices; it does not make them.
A character may always choose against a current score, deity, class discipline, oath, reputation, or personal conviction. The system records what that choice demonstrates and what consequences follow. It never says, “You cannot do that because of your alignment.”
The original four axes still produce one of the existing 81 names, preserving fast D&D-style shorthand without allowing the title to dictate behavior.
Every deity and class provides actionable duties and prohibited conduct instead of a vague moral label.
Characters declare values that can grant resolve when upheld at real cost and create complications when tested.
Convictions, duties, and relationships may be Minor, Major, or Defining rather than equally important.
Personal wants, class discipline, deity covenant, faction obligation, and relationships can conflict without being collapsed into one score.
Eight independent axes describe distinct patterns rather than treating goodness, obedience, mercy, reputation, and self-control as the same thing.
Violating a Defining Conviction creates Strain and forces reflection, repair, replacement, or deliberate abandonment.
What courts, temples, guilds, settlements, and companions believe is tracked separately from inner alignment.
Actions remain possible. The system records movement, covenant effects, reputation, and consequences instead of declaring that a character is forbidden to choose.
Players can see why scores moved, but repeated low-stakes behavior cannot farm alignment, favor, or XP.
